skills.trigger: When evaluating a soft tissue density opacity projected over the lower lung fields on a chest radiograph to determine if it represents an intrapulmonary lesion or an extrapulmonary (chest wall/breast) abnormality.
steps: Inspect the margins of the opacity; extrapulmonary masses (like breast tissue) often have poorly defined or fading superior/lateral borders where they blend into surrounding soft tissues, whereas intrapulmonary masses typically have sharper interfaces against aerated lung.
Trace the density laterally to see if it extends beyond the rib cage contour or connects visibly with the axillary or mammary soft tissue shadow.
Check for the presence of a nipple shadow or skin fold adjacent to the mass, which confirms an external location.

Distinguish from lung pathology by noting that primary lung carcinomas usually present as discrete nodules or masses with distinct borders within the lung parenchyma, unlike the diffuse or ill-defined nature of superimposed breast tissue.

skills.trigger: When characterizing a mass located in the mammary region or lower chest wall to differentiate between benign breast tissue, primary breast carcinoma, and metastatic disease.
steps: Assess the margin definition: poorly defined, irregular, or spiculated margins in the breast region are highly suggestive of primary breast carcinoma.

Evaluate density homogeneity: benign breast proliferation typically appears as homogeneous, symmetric soft tissue density, while malignancy often presents as asymmetric, heterogeneous, or focal density.
Differentiate from metastasis: metastatic disease to the breast/chest wall is rare and usually presents as multiple, well-circumscribed nodules rather than a single poorly defined mass.
Correlate with anatomical landmarks to ensure the 'mass' is not simply normal glandular tissue superimposed on the lung, looking specifically for asymmetry compared to the contralateral side.
